title: Distributed Submodular Subset Selection at Billion Scale
problem: Submodular subset selection for dataset pruning requires materializing all candidate points in a central machine's memory, making it infeasible at billion-point scale.
motivation: Training data curation through submodular maximization can significantly improve model quality, but existing greedy algorithms require O(N) memory on a single node, preventing use with billion-scale datasets common in modern ML pipelines.
method: A distributed bounding algorithm partitions data across workers; each worker computes local upper/lower bounds on marginal gains using grow/shrink steps based on min/max utilities without requiring point-to-point communication. A multi-round partition-based greedy scheme with adaptive repartitioning aggregates global selections. Implemented on Apache Beam for large-scale distributed execution.
key_novelty: Bounding algorithm that avoids centralizing data by computing provably tight bounds on submodular marginal gains in a distributed manner, enabling selection quality approaching centralized greedy without a central memory bottleneck.
contributions: Formal bounding algorithm for distributed submodular maximization with grow/shrink steps
Multi-round partition-based greedy scheme with adaptive repartitioning
Apache Beam implementation scaling to 13 billion data points
98% of centralized greedy quality with 32 communication rounds
Evaluation on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet dataset selection tasks

metrics.accuracy: 98% of centralized greedy quality at 32 communication rounds
metrics.other: Scales to 13 billion points; adaptive partitioning reduces rounds needed

limitations: Quality degrades with fewer communication rounds
Bounding tightness depends on data distribution and partition quality
Apache Beam infrastructure required for large-scale deployment
